# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has always been a fact of urban life, but climate change is transforming a seasonal nuisance into a public health emergency. Cities are inherently hotter than their surroundings—the urban heat island effect can raise urban temperatures by several degrees Fahrenheit compared to nearby rural areas, and the difference is often largest at night, when the human body most needs relief. Heat already kills more Americans in a typical year than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and the toll falls hardest on the poor, the elderly, and those who live in the hottest neighborhoods. The good news is that cities have a substantial toolkit for making heat bearable. The challenge is that every tool involves tradeoffs, and the residents who most need relief are often the least able to pay for it.

## Trees: The Oldest Air Conditioner

The single most effective intervention against urban heat is also the most ancient: shade. A mature street tree can lower surface temperatures beneath its canopy by 20 to 45 degrees Fahrenheit compared to unshaded asphalt. Trees cool through shade and through transpiration, releasing water vapor that acts as a natural air conditioner. They also improve air quality, absorb stormwater, and raise property values.
